dev (mechanic): thanks for the model and year, eli. the hub job needs a wheel removal and a parts check, and we don't have the right internal gear unit on the shelf right now. our distributor's cutoff was 9, so the next delivery we can confirm is thursday morning. we also have two booked brake jobs and a wheel build on the stand today, so the full rebuild isn't something we can take on by 5.

mara (shop lead): eli, i'm sorry, but we can't do the full rebuild and seat installation today. we don't want to promise a turnaround we can't meet, especially with the slipping hub and brake concern. one alternative is to bring it in for a short safety inspection today; we can check the belt tension, hub play, and brake lever feel, then tell you what needs attention before it goes back on the road.

eli (customer): understood, thanks for being straight with me. if you do the inspection, would that include checking the rear brake pads and the hose for a leak? i don't need the seat fitted today if the bike needs to stay in the workshop. i mainly need to know whether it would be safe to ride the five kilometres to the school and back, or if i should arrange another ride.

mara (shop lead): yes, those checks can be part of the inspection, along with a look at the rotor and the belt alignment. to be clear, that's only an assessment, not a promise that we'll be able to repair it today. if anything looks unsafe, we'd ask you not to ride it and talk through options with you. we can start the inspection at 11:30 if that timing works.

dev (mechanic): for planning, the rear brake uses a mineral-oil system, not dot fluid, and the pads are the standard tern gsd shape. i can check what we have once the bike is here, but i haven't set anything aside yet. the seat mount is a separate job; the frame needs the correct adapter plate, so please bring the plate and the seat hardware together if you want us to check compatibility.

eli (customer): i have the adapter plate, two bolts, and the seat with me. the bolts came in a little bag labeled tern, but i don't know if they're the original ones. the bike has a front rack and a rain cover over the child seat right now. should i remove the cover before i bring it in, or can you take a look with it on? also, please let me know if the inspection has a fee.

mara (shop lead): you can leave the cover on for the initial look, but please bring the adapter plate and both bolts loose in the bag so dev can compare them with the frame mounts. the inspection is $35; we charge that even if you decide not to proceed with repairs. if you want the hub work after the parts check, we can discuss a later appointment once we know which unit it needs. i can't confirm a repair date yet.

sana (front desk): i checked the calendar, and there isn't an open repair slot after lunch today. thursday's delivery window is listed as 9 to 12, but that isn't a confirmed arrival time for a specific part. there may be an opening friday afternoon if a customer moves their booking, though nothing is available to reserve against that possibility right now. i'll keep the schedule visible here.

mara (shop lead): for the handoff, let's keep the request and the inspection separate:
1. eli is asking for a full hub rebuild, brake bleed, and child-seat installation today; we're declining that timing.
2. the offered alternative is a $35 inspection at 11:30, including the hub, brake pads, hose, rotor, and belt alignment.
3. any repair or seat fit would need a parts and compatibility check first, and we don't have a repair date to offer yet.
please flag me if i've missed a detail from his call.

eli (customer): that matches what i asked for. before i head over, can you confirm if i need to unload the rear panniers? they're carrying a laptop, two small helmets, and a lock, and i'd rather not leave those on the bike while it's in the stand. i can be there at 11:30, but i still need to work out the school pickup if you recommend not riding it.

noah (mechanic): i'd unload the panniers and keep the helmets and lock with you; it'll make it easier to lift the rear end and check the wheel. we can look at the bike during the inspection, but none of us can tell from the messages alone whether it's safe for that trip. if you have another transport option, it may be worth keeping it open until the mechanic has seen the hub and brake.

mara (shop lead): agreed. eli, please don't treat the inspection slot as clearance to ride; we'll assess it in person and explain what we find before you decide what to do. if you come at 11:30, bring the bike, seat, adapter plate, bolts, and pannier key, and take your valuables off first. the inspection is the only work we can offer today, not the rebuild or installation.

1. site and region
2. object name and date
3. one short sentence about how it was used

Ravi: while you're doing that, could we check the dates on the three objects from the west trench? The draft says 600–500 BCE for all three, but the catalog has 550–450 BCE for the bronze awl. I may be reading an old record.

Maya: I'll ask collections to verify the awl today. Until they confirm, let's not change the date or print the label. The pottery and spindle whorl are listed as 600–500 BCE in the current catalog.

Leah: thanks. For Thursday's access check, I'll bring the large-print draft and the floor plan. Can someone also check glare around 2 p.m.? The west window makes the glass case bright then, and that might affect the label readability too.

Jon: I can be there at two. I'll bring the portable light meter, though we don't need to treat one reading as a final assessment. The blinds were adjusted last month, so let's note their position as well.

Maya: great, thanks. I'll reply to the visitor through the feedback form once we have the label proofs and the sightline notes. For now I can say we're reviewing the map and readability, not that we've made the changes.

Ravi: good. Could we keep the feedbacker's wording anonymous in the design notes? No name was included, but the form has a visit date and party size. We only need the actual comment for this discussion.

Maya: yes, I'll share just the comment, with the date and party details removed. I'll post the proofs here when design sends them, likely Wednesday afternoon. If the awl date isn't confirmed by then, I'll mark that line for review.

Leah: sounds good. I'll reserve Thursday at 10:30 with the access group, and Jon can join at two for the glare check. If either time changes, please update this thread so we don't assume the checks happened.

Jon: done. I'll ask facilities to put down removable tape for the bench trial, not move the bench yet. That gives us a clear position to test and keeps the doorway route open. 🙂

Mara: Quick update for Saturday’s cleanup at Gull Point: last night’s wind pushed a lot of wrack and plastic into the north cove. The public lot is open, but the lower trail is slick, so please use the boardwalk entrance for now.

Dev: I walked the shoreline at lunch. There are fishing lines wrapped around the driftwood near the old lifeguard stand, plus a cracked cooler partly buried in the sand. I didn’t touch either one. Can someone bring work gloves and a sturdy pair of cutters?

Nia: I can bring gloves, cutters, and the orange buckets from the storage shed. The shed key is with me. I’m not sure whether the little blue cart still has a working wheel, though, so we may need to carry supplies by hand.

Owen: The tide chart says the water will be coming in around 10:40. We should probably start at the north end and work toward the picnic area, but I’d like a second set of eyes on that plan before we send it out.

Mara: That makes sense. The county notice says the access gate must stay clear at all times, and the ranger asked us not to stack full bags beside it. We’ll need a pickup spot farther uphill, away from the marked dune plants.

Luis: I can bring my hatchback, but I can’t take loose glass or anything leaking in the car. Is anyone able to bring a lined tote for the glass? I’ve got two thick contractor bags for ordinary litter and wet rope.

Priya: I have a plastic storage bin we can use for glass, and I’ll label it before we leave. There’s also a small box of paper tags in the supply cabinet if we want to mark anything that needs a ranger’s attention.

Tess: One thing I noticed yesterday: a few pieces that look like foam are actually attached to the old dock bumpers. I don’t know if those are still in use, so let’s leave them where they are and ask the ranger before pulling anything loose.

Dev: Good call. I’ll message Rowan at the ranger station and ask whether the bumper pieces should stay put. I can also check if they want the tangled fishing line brought to the office or set aside in a separate bag.

Nia: For the volunteer note, can we say closed-toe shoes are strongly recommended, and that people should bring water? There’s no drinking fountain at the cove, and the nearest shop is a good walk from the lot.

Owen: Yes, and maybe mention that the cleanup is still on if the forecast stays as it is now. The weather app shows scattered showers in the afternoon, but that could change. We should check again Friday evening before calling anything off.

Mara: I’ll update the signup post with the boardwalk entrance, the tide window, and the water reminder. I’ll keep the wording tentative about the weather. If the lower trail dries out, we can ask the ranger whether it’s okay to use it later.

Luis: I can arrive around 8:30 and put cones by the uphill pickup spot, as long as that doesn’t block the maintenance lane. Could someone confirm which side of the picnic shelter is best? I don’t want bags sitting where families walk through.

Priya: The shelter’s east side has a wide gravel strip, but there’s a storm drain at the far end. We should keep bags well back from that and avoid leaving anything where runoff could carry it toward the water.

Tess: Here’s a quick list of what I can cover:
1. Bring a first-aid kit and extra water.
2. Take photos of large or unusual debris without moving it.
3. Keep the path to the gate clear while bags are collected.

Dev: I just heard back from Rowan. They said to leave anything attached to the dock structure alone, and to set loose fishing line in a separate, clearly marked bag. They haven’t confirmed the pickup spot yet, so we still need to check that part.

Nia: Thanks. I’ll bring a roll of bright tape for the fishing-line bag and a small grabber for wrappers near the boardwalk. I won’t use it around the nesting signs; we should leave that whole marked area undisturbed.

Owen: Does anyone have spare work gloves in a medium size? We’ve got several large pairs in the shed, but I couldn’t find any smaller ones this morning. A couple of the volunteers on the list asked about sizing.

Priya — 6:48 am: I ran past at 6:10 and there was orange mesh across the entrance, no sign that I could read from the sidewalk. The north trailhead is open, but it adds about 1.4 miles to the loop.

Maya — 6:51 am: yep, creek gate. I didn’t see a posted notice either. Three newer runners were waiting by the bus stop and one left when nobody knew where to go. Can someone help me check the alternate route today?

Ben — 6:55 am: I can check after work, around 5:30. The map in our club folder is old though; it still shows the footbridge by the soccer fields, which was closed last winter after the railing got loose.

Rosa — 6:58 am: i have the updated county map saved. Footbridge is marked closed through June, and the gravel service lane behind the tennis courts is not a public path, even if it looks like a shortcut.

Dev — 7:03 am: good catch. For saturday we could meet at the library instead, then take Willow Ave to the north trailhead. Sidewalk is narrow for a big group, but there’s a crossing signal at 8th.

Maya — 7:07 am: library lot might work, but the farmers market sets up there at 7 and the east half fills fast. I can ask the library desk if club parking is okay before their doors open.

Omar — 7:12 am: I’m nearby now. Library lot has cones over 12 spaces and a market van unloading; there are still maybe 20 spaces on the west side. No paper notice about other events.

Nina — 7:16 am: could we move the start to the school lot on Juniper? It’s 0.6 miles from the trail entrance and has bathrooms. We’d need permission, though, and I don’t know who handles weekend access.

Leo — 7:20 am: I emailed the school office last fall about using that lot for the food drive. The auto reply says the office is closed on weekends; it doesn’t say whether the gate stays unlocked.

Priya — 7:24 am: also, the north entrance has a water fountain but it’s been turned off before April in past years. I can bring two refill jugs, though they only fit in my hatchback if I fold one seat down.

Ben — 7:29 am: I’ll bring my wagon for the jugs and first-aid kit. Does anyone know if the new route has a place for the 9:00 beginners group to wait without blocking the bike lane?

1) library to 8th Street crossing is about 0.3 mile, mostly flat, but the curb ramp on the south side is cracked.
2) 8th to Willow Ave has a narrow sidewalk for one block; runners should stay single file there.
3) north trailhead has a gravel lot, two benches, and a map board, but no reliable water or toilets.
4) from the trailhead we can use the yellow loop for 3 miles; the blue spur is muddy near the drainage ditch, so skip that one for now.

Rosa — 7:39 am: I walked the yellow loop Tuesday. The first half is packed dirt and the last quarter mile has loose stones; my ankle was fine in road shoes, but it’s rougher than the old creek path.

Dev — 7:43 am: thanks. We usually have 18 to 25 people, with two dogs some weeks. If we take the sidewalk in a single group, we’ll stretch past the signal. Maybe split by pace before leaving the library?

Maya — 7:47 am: yeah, that’s probably safer. I can bring the pace cards, but our laminated set is missing the 11-minute one. Is anyone able to print a replacement before friday?

Nina — 7:52 am: i can print it at home. Also, I have six reflective vests in my car, but the elastic on two is stretched out. I’ll bring all six and mark the bad ones with tape.

Omar — 7:58 am: one more thing: the route crosses the bike lane at Willow, and traffic was pretty quick at 6:30 today. A volunteer at the front and back could help, but we shouldn’t stop runners in the lane.

Leo — 8:04 am: agreed. I can be rear sweeper for the easy group. I’ve got a whistle, but the battery light on my headlamp is unreliable, so I’ll bring my spare clip light instead.

Priya — 8:10 am: I’m happy to lead the steady group if we keep the pace around 10:30 to 11:00. I can’t stay after 9:15, and I don’t want anyone assuming I’m available to drive people home.

Ben — 8:15 am: understood, no ride promises. I can lead the faster group and wait at the trailhead for the second group before we start the loop. My knee is okay for 3 miles, not the extra spur.

Maya — 8:21 am: we should also message the people who aren’t in this channel. Last week’s signup sheet has 31 names, but some only come once a month; can someone draft a short update that doesn’t sound like the gate is permanently closed?

Rosa — 8:26 am: I’ll write it. We should say the east gate is locked today, the county notice we saw said work begins monday, and we’re checking the alternate meetup. That leaves room for the schedule to change.

Dev — 8:31 am: I can check the county site at lunch and call the trail office if there’s a number listed. If the route status is unclear, I’d rather we use the park perimeter path than guess about access.

Maya — 8:37 am: good. Can two people help with the Saturday check? We need someone to confirm library parking and someone to walk the crossing and trail entrance around 7:15. Please reply here if you can.

Omar — 8:41 am: I can do the crossing check at 7:15. I’ll take a photo of the curb ramp and the map board, but I won’t post pictures of any runners without asking first.

Nina — 8:46 am: I can call the library today. If they say no parking, I’ll ask whether the market has a designated overflow lot nearby; I don’t want to promise the school lot until we hear back.

Leo — 8:51 am: can we keep the regular 6:30 start time for now? Some folks take the bus and plan around it. We can send the update tonight, then send a correction if the parking answer changes.

Maya — 8:56 am: yes, keep 6:30 for now and meet at the library west side unless Nina hears otherwise. morning, quick update on the Bellwether table cover. we opened the folded edge yesterday and found a second layer of plain linen under the blue wool, not another patch. The wool is brittle along the west border, but the center still flexes. I took photos with the scale and color card; they're in the restoration folder, under April 18.

Jonah — 9:19 AM
thanks, Mara. I looked at the close-ups. Is that pale line near the corner a stitch channel or a crease? In the room photo it looks straight, but the detail shot seems to bend toward the fringe. I don't want us calling it a seam until we can check it under the scope.

Leila — 9:27 AM
I think it's a crease, though I'm not certain. The linen layer has a narrow fold there and the wool nap changes direction at about the same point. The old inventory says “blue border repaired,” with no date or thread description. Could be referring to this area, could be another repair entirely.

Mara — 9:34 AM
that's how I read it too. We haven't lifted the wool anywhere else, since the adhesive residue gets powdery when the room is dry. The humidifier log shows 46% yesterday afternoon and 42% overnight, so I paused before putting any weight on the edge.

Nico — 9:43 AM
For context, the back is supported on washed cotton muslin, pinned to the padded board at 6 cm intervals. There are 3 loose pins along the short side, but none under the damaged border. The board is level, and the cover hasn't moved since we brought it in on Monday.

Priya — 9:51 AM
I checked the thread samples from the storage envelope. The blue one is probably wool, not silk, but the label just says “border, 1978?” with a question mark. The cream thread has a synthetic shine. We shouldn't assume either sample came from this cover, even though they're in the same envelope.

Jonah — 10:03 AM
One thing: the fringe is still attached at both ends, but the middle 11 cm is loose. I counted 14 visible warp ends there. A few are tucked under the folded linen, and I can't tell yet whether they were stitched down or just caught in the fold.

Tess — 10:31 AM

Nico — 10:42 AM

Priya — 10:54 AM

Mara — 11:06 AM

Jonah — 11:17 AM

Leila — 11:29 AM

Hey team — I’m putting together next month’s local history newsletter, and I’m looking at the old Riverside footbridge for our short “Then and Now” feature. The county opened it in 1936, and it connected the mill district with the bus stop on Alder Street. A few readers have mentioned that people used to gather there on summer evenings, but I haven’t found anything in the archive that confirms it.

I’ve got a photo from the 1950s that shows a small crowd by the railing, though there’s no date or note on the back. I’m thinking we could pair it with a recent photo from the same spot and ask readers to share memories. We should probably be clear that the gathering story is still unconfirmed, rather than presenting it as fact. If anyone has a clipping, family photo, or a name for someone who might remember the bridge, that’d be really helpful.

Does anyone know whether the historical society has a better-dated copy of that photo, or another source about how the bridge was used? Mara: got some feedback from Sunday's event, sharing it here before we reply. the customer wrote, "I love the shop and the staff were kind, but the reading felt crowded and I couldn't hear the questions from the back. I hope you'll try it again with more chairs and a mic."

Jo: that's useful, and pretty fair. we had 31 people in the front room, right? the event page said seating was limited, but maybe that didn't tell folks what it actually felt like once they arrived.

Mara: yeah, 31 signed in, plus two people who came in late and didn't want to add their names. we had 24 chairs out. the rest were standing by the poetry shelves or near the door.

Dev: i was by the register for the first half. from there, i could hear the author, but the questions were hard to catch. people kept turning around to look at whoever was speaking.

Jo: we did offer the small meeting room, but the author wanted to be surrounded by the new releases. i don't think we should suggest the other room in our reply like that would've solved everything.

Mara: agreed. let's acknowledge the crowding and sound, and thank them for saying something. no need to promise a mic until we check what we have and whether it works in that room.

Dev: the little speaker in the office has a mic input, i think. haven't tested it since we used it for the winter book drive, and the cable might be missing.

Jo: i can test it tuesday before opening. if it doesn't work, i'll ask the library if they still lend out their portable setup. that'd be a question, not a plan yet.

Mara: good. i also want to be careful with the chair part. we can fit a few more if we move the display table, but the aisle to the back door needs to stay clear.

hey folks, quick bench update on the little temperature display. i soldered the header pins onto the sensor board last night, and mounted the screen on a scrap piece of acrylic. the screen is 0.96 inch, 128 by 64, and the sensor is a bme280 i had in the parts drawer. i powered it from the usb port on my laptop, not the bench supply, so the wiring is still pretty simple.

the first reading came up about 1.8 degrees c higher than the room thermometer, but both were sitting in different spots on the desk. i'll leave them side by side for a while before i change anything. the display refreshes every two seconds right now, which is probably more often than it needs to.

i haven't put the board in an enclosure yet. the acrylic is just a temporary mount, and one corner is a little rough from the handsaw. i have a small project box here, but it may be too shallow once the usb cable is plugged in. does anyone know if these boxes usually have enough room for a right-angle cable? i can measure the clearance after work and post it here. no photos yet; i forgot to bring the phone stand to the bench.","response":"Hey folks, quick bench update on the little temperature display. lena: hey all, starting a thread for the May trip so we stop losing details in texts. We’re looking at May 22–27, driving from Portland to Vancouver and then over to Victoria. It’s six of us: Ravi and me, Noah (9), Mira (5), my mom Diane, and Priya. Nothing is booked yet except our aquarium tickets for Saturday.

ravi: I checked the calendar again, and Friday the 22nd is the first day we can all leave. I can take the Subaru, but with six people and bags it’ll be tight. The kids can share the back seat, and Diane says she’s fine in the passenger seat, but we still need to decide what to do with the luggage.

priya: I can bring my small duffel and a backpack, no hard suitcase. I’d rather not rent a second car unless we really need one. If we drive all the way, can we leave Portland by 7:00 a.m.? That should get us to the border before the afternoon traffic, though I’m not sure how much time to add for the crossing.

diane: I’m happy to leave early, but I don’t want to be rushed through breakfast. Could we pack sandwiches the night before and stop somewhere after we cross? I’d also like one proper stretch break for my knee. It’s okay on long drives as long as I get out and walk every couple of hours.

lena: For Vancouver, I found a hotel near Coal Harbour that has two queen beds and a pullout sofa. It’s $318 Canadian a night before tax, and parking is another $42 a night. The room says it sleeps six, but I haven’t called to check whether they count Mira as a full guest. Free cancellation ends May 8.

ravi: That’s more than I expected, but it’s walking distance to the aquarium and the seawall. The cheaper place by the airport is $229 a night, although we’d have to drive in and pay for parking downtown. I can call both hotels at lunch and ask about the bed setup, breakfast, and whether the parking price includes in-and-out privileges.

noah: is the aquarium really booked for 10:30 saturday? i want to see the penguins first and the jellyfish room. also can we get lunch there or should we bring snacks because i get hungry before noon

lena: Yes, the tickets are for 10:30 a.m. on Saturday, May 23. We can stay as long as we like, and I think there’s a café, but I haven’t checked the menu or prices. We should bring a couple of snacks in case the line is long. We’re not adding Science World this time; that would be too much for one day.

priya: On Sunday we could take the 11:00 ferry from Tsawwassen to Swartz Bay, then drive to Victoria. The sailing is about an hour and 35 minutes, but we’d need to arrive early with the car. I saw a fare estimate of $112 for the vehicle and two adults, plus $18 for each extra adult. Kids are less, but I didn’t get the exact amount.

ravi: Can you send the page you used? I saw a different total when I looked, and I’m not sure if it included the reservation fee. I’d rather book a specific sailing than risk lining up, especially with the kids and the bags. We need to leave enough time to check out of the hotel and get to Tsawwassen too.

lena: Here’s what I have so far for the middle of the trip:
1. Friday, May 22: drive Portland to Vancouver; check in and have an easy dinner.
2. Saturday, May 23: aquarium at 10:30; keep the afternoon open for the seawall or a rest.
3. Sunday, May 24: check out, ferry to Victoria, and pick up groceries on the way to the hotel.

priya: I like keeping Sunday light. The hotel in Victoria is a guesthouse near Cook Street Village, $274 Canadian a night for a family suite. It has a small kitchenette and breakfast is not included. They have one parking space per room, but the listing says we have to confirm the Subaru’s height because the garage clearance is low.

diane: The kitchenette would help, and I can make oatmeal for the kids if there’s a pot and bowls. I don’t need a fancy breakfast. Can you ask if the suite is on the ground floor? Stairs are manageable, but I’d rather not carry my suitcase up two flights if there’s another option.

ravi: I messaged the guesthouse this morning. They said the suite is on the second floor, but there’s an elevator. They haven’t confirmed the garage height yet; they asked for the vehicle model, so I sent Subaru Outback, 2021. They said they’ll reply by tomorrow. Cancellation is free until May 12.

lena: For Monday, May 25, the kids want the Royal BC Museum and the harbour. The museum is open until 5, but I can’t tell if we’ll need timed tickets. We could go in the morning, have lunch nearby, and leave the afternoon for Beacon Hill Park if the weather’s decent. No need to cram in Butchart Gardens too.

noah: can we go to the park with the goats? my friend said there are goats at beacon hill and i want to see them. also i want to bring my soccer ball but it might be too big for the car

priya: Beacon Hill has a petting zoo, but their site says it opens seasonally, so we should check the hours for that week. I can bring a small ball instead of the full-size one. For the museum, I didn’t see timed entry on the ticket page, but I only looked quickly. Maybe someone can verify before we buy anything.

diane: Tuesday the 26th could be a slower day. I’d like to walk around the Inner Harbour in the morning and sit somewhere for coffee. If everyone wants to see another garden or shop, I can take a break at the hotel and meet up later. I don’t want the schedule to assume I’m doing every activity.

ravi: Agreed. We should also work out the return route for Wednesday, May 27. The ferry from Victoria back to Tsawwassen is about 1 hour and 35 minutes, then it’s a long drive to Portland. There’s a Coho ferry to Port Angeles, but that adds a border crossing and a different route. I haven’t compared the prices or departure times yet.

lena: I’m leaning toward returning through Tsawwassen because it’s the route we already know, but I’m open to the Coho if it saves a meaningful amount of driving. We should plan a real meal and a break on the way home, not just hope the kids sleep. I can take the first driving shift if we leave early.

priya: I can handle the food list and bring a cooler, but we should agree on how many hotel nights we’re paying for. I counted two in Vancouver and three in Victoria, so five nights total. If we decide to add a night in Vancouver, that changes the ferry day and the hotel price. I don’t think we’ve agreed to that.

diane: Five nights works for me. Please don’t book a room with only one bathroom without checking first; that’s important with six people getting ready in the morning. I can share with Priya if the suite has two separate sleeping areas, but I’d like to know the actual layout before we pay a deposit.

ravi: I’ll put the booking details in one place once we hear from the hotels. For now, we have the aquarium tickets, but no hotel, ferry, museum, or garden tickets. The main open things seem to be the car space, exact room setup, and the return ferry. Tell me if I missed something.

lena: Specific question for everyone: should I try to reserve the larger Vancouver hotel and the Tsawwassen ferry first, or wait until we confirm the Victoria suite’s garage clearance and room layout? We have $1,600 set aside for lodging and ferries before food, and I don’t want to spend it in the wrong order. Mara: Thanks for the detailed ride notes, Jules. Your point about the front truck feeling twitchy on the cracked path is useful. We’d been testing on smooth pavement, so we weren’t seeing that same movement. I’m pulling the setup notes into this thread so we can compare the changes clearly.

Jules: Yep, the rough section by the old rail bridge is where I noticed it most. At about 18 mph, the board wandered when I crossed the seams. It wasn’t a speed wobble, exactly; it just took more small corrections than my other setup. The rear felt planted the whole time.

Mara: Got it. You also mentioned that the board was easier to pump after you changed the front bushings. Which ones did you swap in? I have the stock 90a barrels listed on your original build sheet, but I don’t want to assume those were still on the board during the ride.

Jules: I put in the 87a roadside bushings from the spare kit, with the stock roadside washers. The boardside barrels are still 90a. I tightened the kingpin nut about a quarter turn after the first run, then backed it off a little when the return felt slow.

Devin: That’s a helpful detail. The truck has a 50-degree baseplate, and a softer roadside bushing can make the steering feel more responsive without changing the baseplate angle. A quarter turn can also be a noticeable adjustment on that setup. Did you keep the same wheel wells and risers as before?

Jules: Yes, same 1/8-inch risers and the 70 mm wheels. I didn’t get any wheel bite, even when I leaned hard through the parking-lot turns. The wheels are the 78a ones, not the 80a set from the photos. I should’ve called that out earlier.

mira: hey folks, i'm stuck on a little 12v led controller i built for the workbench and could use a second set of eyes. it's an esp32 dev board driving a 1.5 meter warm-white strip through an irlZ44N mosfet, with a 12v 3a wall supply. the strip is fine if i connect it directly, but when i run the controller above about 60% brightness the mosfet gets too hot to keep a finger on, and the esp32 sometimes reboots. at low brightness it mostly works, though there’s a faint flicker. i’m not sure if i made a wiring mistake or if the mosfet is just a bad choice.
owen: what are you using for the gate resistor and pulldown? also, does the esp32 share ground with the 12v supply? the irlz44n isn't a great logic-level part at 3.3v, so that might be part of it, but i'd check the wiring before swapping parts. my first little strip project had the power grounds separate and it acted really weird. do you have a photo or a sketch of the connections?
mira: grounds are connected at the supply input, then one wire goes to the esp32 ground and another to the strip negative. i put a 220 ohm resistor between gpio 18 and the gate, and a 10k from gate to ground. there's about 25 cm of jumper wire between the board and the mosfet because i mounted it near the strip connector. no heatsink right now. i used the parts i had in the drawer, and the listing for the mosfet called it logic level, but i didn't check the datasheet until last night.
rae: yeah, the name is misleading there. the datasheet's low on-resistance number is given at a 10v gate drive, not 3.3v. that doesn't automatically explain the reboot, but it could explain the heat. are you switching the strip on the low side, with its positive wire straight to 12v and its negative wire going to the mosfet drain? and what frequency are you using for pwm? some esp32 examples use a pretty high default, which can make an already marginal setup warmer.
mira: wiring is low side like you described. the strip positive is on 12v, strip negative goes to drain, and source goes back to supply ground. pwm is 5 khz from the ledc setup. i checked the board's 3v3 pin with a cheap meter while it was running; it sits around 3.27v until i turn brightness up, then it dips briefly to maybe 3.05v when the board resets. i'm powering the esp32 from usb on my laptop, not from the 12v supply. could the usb cable be part of this?
owen: possible, especially if the laptop port or cable is marginal, but i'd be suspicious of ground bounce or noise too. a meter can miss a really short dip. try a short usb cable and a different port if that's easy, and keep the strip current path away from the esp32 ground wire. also, what's the strip's current at full brightness? a 3a supply doesn't mean the strip is actually drawing 3a, and a thin jumper on the return path can get warm or cause voltage drop.
mira: i measured about 1.1a at full brightness with my inline meter, and around 0.7a at the level where the mosfet starts getting hot. the jumper wires are the usual dupont ones, maybe 22 awg, and the strip leads are a little thicker. i haven't checked their temperature yet. for context, the mosfet is on a small solderless breadboard right now, not a permanent board. i know that's not ideal for current, but i thought 1a would be okay for a quick test.
jules: i'd move the power wiring off the breadboard before doing more full-brightness tests. the breadboard contacts and dupont leads aren't a great path for strip current, even if the current sounds modest. the long gate lead can also pick up noise. put the mosfet close to the strip connector, use short heavier wires for 12v and the return, and leave the esp32 ground connection short. don't leave it running unattended while it's getting hot. did you verify the pinout on that exact package? different mosfets can look similar.
mira: good point, i'll check the package marking against the datasheet. i had assumed the pins were gate, drain, source left to right when the text faces me, but i didn't confirm that. i also found a 100 nf ceramic capacitor and a 470 uf electrolytic in my parts box. would adding those near the strip connector help, or should i first move everything off the breadboard and retest? i'm trying to change one thing at a time so i can tell what actually fixes it.
rae: i'd confirm the pinout and rebuild the high-current path first; the capacitor isn't a substitute for that. the 470 uf across the 12v and ground near the strip may help with supply dips, and the 100 nf can help with high-frequency noise, but check the electrolytic's polarity and voltage rating. i'd also try a mosfet specified for low resistance at 2.5v or 3.3v gate drive. if it still reboots, measure the supply at the board during switching if you can. post what you find when you've tested it; i'm curious whether the heat changes after the wiring move.","response":"MODE: /slack

2. Keep the library’s front steps free of bags and chairs.
3. Bring a light jacket; the courtyard gets breezy after sunset.

mara: quick pond update from saturday: the water was clear at the edge, but there was a thin green film on the shallow shelf by the west stones. the pump was still running, and the return had a steady flow. i didn't see any fish gasping or hanging near the surface.

inez: i checked the basket before lunch. it had maple seeds, two bits of willow leaf, and a lot of fine string algae, mostly caught on the lower side. the basket wasn't packed tight, so i rinsed it in a bucket of pond water and put it back.

dev: the thermometer read 18 c at 9:20 am, in the shade near the bench. that's a little cooler than last weekend, when it was 20 c around the same time. i wrote both readings on the card inside the shed.

mara: i also lifted the pump cover to look for blockage. there was one oak leaf across the intake slots, nothing wound around the impeller. i shut the pump off first, cleared the leaf, then switched it back on and checked the return.

leo: nice. did the skimmer float freely after that? ours sometimes sticks against the liner if the water drops, and then it misses the bits that collect on the far side.

inez: it floated fine when i checked at 11. water level was about 3 cm below the stone mark, same as friday. the top-up hose is still coiled by the tap; i didn't add water because the level hasn't moved much.

sam: i trimmed back the mint that had started leaning over the north rim. took off four long stems and left the short growth in the pot. there were a few bees on the flowers, so i waited till they moved before cutting.

dev: on the water test, ph was 7.4 and the strip looked between 0 and 1 ppm for nitrite. nitrate was about 10 ppm. i might have held the strip in the light too long, though, so those are rough readings, not a new baseline.

mara: small maintenance list for next visit:
1. brush the algae from the shallow shelf, without scraping the liner.
2. check the pump basket again after the leaves drop.
3. look at the air stone; it was bubbling, but the bubbles seemed uneven on one side.

leo: i can bring the soft pond brush. last time it loosened the film without lifting the gravel, as long as i worked toward the drain and didn't press hard. i'll keep the brush separate from the patio scrubber.

inez: please don't brush the whole shelf in one go. there are two small snails near the flat rock, and i saw one tadpole under the ledge. we can leave that corner alone for now and do the open section only.

sam: good point. i saw the same snails on sunday, just below the water line. i didn't move them. the tadpole was still there when i left, but i couldn't tell if there were others farther under the ledge.

dev: the air pump noise is about the same as last month, a low hum with a brief rattle when it starts. the hose isn't kinked, and the plug stayed dry. i didn't open the housing because it was working normally after the first few seconds.

mara: one thing i noticed: the water was lower on the south edge than it looked from the path, but the stones were dry outside and there wasn't a wet patch around the pond. could just be the slight slope in that section.

tess: i checked the log photos from the past three saturdays. the level mark looks nearly unchanged in all of them, and the south edge has that same gap under the flat stone. i'll take another photo from the bench next time for comparison.

leo: the heron decoy is still by the shed, not beside the pond. i left it there because it kept falling over in the wind last week. no heron sightings since thursday, and the fish were visible when i walked around at dusk.

inez: for the plants, the yellow flag iris has one new leaf and no yellowing at the base. the water lily has two pads with small brown edges, but the rest look firm. i removed one loose, damaged pad that was already floating.

Maya: hey folks, could use a second opinion on my backyard pond. it's roughly 8 by 5 feet and about 22 inches deep at the center, with a shallow shelf around one side. we put it in last spring, and it has a small waterfall, a pump rated for 900 gallons an hour, and a box filter. the water's been going green again since the weather warmed up. does anyone have suggestions for what to check before i change the setup?

Leo: what kind of fish are in there, and do you know the actual water volume? those dimensions can be misleading with the shelf. also, is the filter the one that came with the pond kit? my neighbor's kit had a tiny sponge in the box, even though the pump itself was decent.

Maya: three goldfish, all around 3 to 4 inches long. i haven't calculated the volume because the shelf takes up more space than i expected. the kit is a PondPro 900, and the filter has foam plus a little bag of ceramic rings. i rinsed the foam under the hose once last month, which i now realize might've been a bad idea.

Priya: yeah, i'd avoid tap water on the filter media next time, since chlorine can affect the bacteria. when i clean mine, i squeeze the foam gently in a bucket of pond water. are you seeing string algae on the stones too, or is it mostly the water looking cloudy and green?

Maya: mostly green water, though there's a thin layer of stringy stuff on the rocks by the waterfall. i can still see the bottom shelf in the morning, but by late afternoon it's hard to make out. i haven't added any algaecide. the fish are eating normally, and i haven't noticed them gasping at the surface.

Jon: how much direct sun does that corner get? ours gets about six hours, and the water went green every summer until we planted a small water lily. not saying that's the whole fix, just asking because your pond gets afternoon sun, right? a photo might help show the shade around it.

Maya: probably seven hours, from about 10:30 until 5:30. there's a fence on the west side but it doesn't shade the pond until evening. the lily basket is on the shelf, and the leaves cover maybe a quarter of the surface so far. i can send a picture after work.

Rae: one thing to check is whether the filter is rated for ponds with fish, not just the pump flow. the label on my old box said 900 gallons per hour, but that was pump flow with no lift; the waterfall height cut it down. how high is yours, measured from the water to the outlet?

Maya: the outlet is about 18 inches above the pond, and the tubing makes one bend behind the rocks. it's 1-inch tubing, about six feet long. the waterfall still looks steady to me, but i haven't measured how much water actually comes out. the filter box says it's for ponds up to 1,000 gallons, though.

Leo: could be worth checking the media and the flow together. i wouldn't assume the pond is 1,000 gallons just from the label, especially with the shelf and the shallow edges. do you have a test kit, or have you had the water tested recently? ammonia and nitrite would be useful to know with fish in there.

Maya: i have strips from the garden center, not the dropper kit. last saturday they looked like zero for nitrite and somewhere between zero and 0.5 for nitrate, but the colors are hard to match. the package doesn't test ammonia. i also have a thermometer; water was 72°F around noon.

Priya: strips can be a little tricky to read, especially if the light's changing. if you use them again, maybe compare the colors indoors with the chart beside them. do you know your tap water's pH, and do you top the pond up often? our water is pretty hard, so topping up changes things slowly over summer.

Maya: i top it up about once a week, maybe 3 or 4 inches after evaporation. our town water report lists moderate hardness, but i haven't tested the tap myself. the pond has a liner, and there's no obvious leak around the edges. rainwater from the shed roof doesn't run into it.

Nora: a numbered checklist may make it easier to figure out what changed. here's what i'd write down before changing anything: 1) pond temperature and test readings, 2) how long the pump runs, 3) whether the filter foam is clogged, and 4) how much of the surface is shaded. do you run the pump overnight too?

Maya: yes, it's on all day and all night, including through winter. i cleaned the little prefilter screen last weekend because it had leaves in it, and the flow picked up afterward. the box filter sits beside the pond under a flat stone, so it's shaded but not buried. i haven't opened it since rinsing the foam.

Rae: that gives you a few useful details to compare, and the photo will help with the plants and waterfall. how often do you feed the fish, and what do you do with the clippings when you trim the lily? i ask because leftover food and decaying plant bits can add to the load, even when the water looks fine.

Maya: they get a small pinch once each morning, and usually finish it in under a minute. i trimmed two yellow lily leaves last week and took them out right away. there's also a mesh basket with a few marginal plants on the shelf, but their roots haven't filled it yet.

Jon: got it. if you can share the pond photo, the filter label, and your best estimate of the volume, folks can look at the whole setup rather than guessing from pump flow alone. i'm also curious whether the green color appeared gradually or changed noticeably after the warm spell. when did you first see it?","response":"MODE: /slack

theo: Ansonia used a lot of different labels, so i'd treat the paper date as a clue, not a firm date for the whole clock. Is there a date or patent line on the movement plate? Also, photos of the dial, hands and case corners might help narrow down the style. The company made loads of mantel clocks over a long stretch.

mara: i can get photos after work. the face is about 5 inches across, white enamel with black Roman numerals, and the minute hand has a little bend near the tip. case is roughly 11 inches tall. the seller said it ran when she was a kid, which doesn't tell us much, i know.

june: Check the bottom and the inside of the back panel too. Sometimes there’s a paper label tucked under the movement, or a penciled number on the wood. Don't scrape anything off to find it, though. Old paper can be fragile, and the label you found may be useful even if it isn't a date.

luis: On mine the movement plate has the maker name and patent dates, but they weren't the year mine was assembled. If yours has a gong coil, see if there’s a maker mark on that as well. I wouldn't use the gong or movement number by itself to date the case; parts can get changed.

mara: good point about the case and movement not necessarily matching. there's a brass gong at the back, one winding key in the drawer and two little holes on the dial, at 4 and 8. no key marked on the case. the back panel's loose at the top, so i'm trying not to handle it more than i need to.

eLI: For the winding holes, check that the key fits without forcing it. Some old keys are the wrong size, and a key can slip and scratch the dial. If it turns freely, that's one thing; if it catches or feels gritty, stop. A clock that's been sitting may need attention before anyone tries to run it.

theo: Also, don't assume the little bend in the minute hand is damage from use. It may have been bent at some point to clear something, or it could just be a bend. I'd avoid trying to straighten it while it's on the dial. A close photo from straight on would show whether the hands touch.

nina: If you're going to take the movement out, take a few pictures first and keep the screws in a labeled bag. But honestly, if you've never done one, I'd leave it in place for now. The wood case and the enamel dial can be cleaned very differently, and a general cleaner could do more harm than good.

mara: here's what i've noticed so far, in case it's useful: 1) the oak has a dark finish, worn lighter along the right front edge; 2) the glass door has a small chip at the bottom left; 3) the dial has a hairline mark from about 7 toward the center; 4) the pendulum is present, but i haven't tried hanging it.

Mara: quick update from the clock room: we finished the first pass through the estate lot this morning. Jon: The tall oak longcase is marked “J. H. Evans, Bristol” on the dial. Its brass weights and pendulum were wrapped separately in brown paper, and we found the winding key in the bottom drawer. Mara: For the record, the blue transferware mantel clock is the one with the loose rear panel, not the clock in the green box. We’ve kept both boxes beside their clocks and added matching paper tags, so they won’t get separated during the room move.

Owen: I measured the walnut wall clock at 74 centimeters high, 31 wide, and 14 deep. Mara: Here’s the room-by-room list for the next inventory pass:
1. East cabinet: six mantel clocks, two boxed parts trays, and the loose winding keys.
2. North wall: four wall clocks, including the walnut clock Owen measured.

4. Alcove: five longcase or bracket clocks, with the oak case and brass bracket clock noted separately.

Mara: Thanks for the thoughtful feedback on my post about building a small vinyl collection. I’m replying here because a few people asked about the setup, and Leon’s note about storage deserves more than a quick thumbs-up. I’ve added a numbered section below with the changes I’m considering.

Mara: That’s a good point. I’ve got about 140 records in a low oak shelf, and I keep the heavier gatefolds on the bottom row. I’ll mention that a shelf should stay level and support the collection without leaning against a radiator or a sunny window.

Priya: Could you also say how you decide which records to clean? I don’t wash every used LP automatically, but I do brush it before playing. A record can look clean and still have dust in the grooves, especially after sitting in a paper inner sleeve.

Mara: Yes, that distinction is helpful. My routine is a carbon-fiber brush before each side, then a wet clean for records that are visibly dirty or noisy. I use distilled water with the cleaning solution, and I let the record dry fully before putting it away.

Eli: I liked the part about buying slowly. The local shop’s dollar bin is fun, but I’ve brought home albums I only recognized from the cover. Maybe say that a low price doesn’t turn a record into a must-have; it still needs to be music you want to hear.

Mara: I can add that. I’m trying to collect records I’ll actually play, not fill a shelf by the end of the month. I still browse the cheap bin, but now I check the artist, label, pressing details, and condition before I decide.

Tess: Your photos show the records standing upright, which is great. A couple of beginners in our listening group asked whether leaning is okay for a short time. I’d say to avoid it when possible, since pressure between tightly packed jackets can cause problems over time.

Mara: Agreed. I’ll keep the wording practical and not make it sound like one brief lean ruins a record. Mine are snug enough not to slump, but I can still slide one out without tugging the neighboring sleeves.

Leon: The tracking spreadsheet section made me smile. I use a notebook instead, and I write down the shop, price, and anything I noticed about the copy. It’s saved me from buying the same pressing twice when the labels looked different.

Mara: That’s exactly the sort of detail I’d like to include. My sheet has artist, title, label, catalog number, condition, date, and price. I leave pressing notes blank when I can’t verify them, rather than guessing from a quick search.

Priya: One small request: could you explain that grading is an estimate, not a guarantee? Two copies marked VG+ at different shops can sound very different. I’ve had better luck asking to inspect the record than relying on a sticker alone.

Mara: Definitely. I’ll say that grading language varies between sellers, and it’s worth checking the actual record when the shop allows it. If I’m buying online, I look for clear photos and a return policy before paying.

Eli: On the budget point, I’d mention sleeves as a recurring cost. Inner sleeves aren’t expensive one at a time, but replacing a whole stack adds up. I switched to archival-style inners gradually instead of trying to redo the collection in one weekend.

Mara: Good catch. I did the same, starting with records I played most often. I keep the original printed inner sleeves with the jacket when they’re in decent shape, and use a separate protective sleeve for the record itself.

Tess: I also appreciated that you didn’t treat streaming as the enemy. I listen digitally before I buy something unfamiliar, then look for a copy if the album sticks with me. That’s made my purchases more intentional and cut down on impulse buys.

Mara: That’s part of my approach too. There’s no single right way to enjoy music, and a collection doesn’t need to be large to feel personal. I’ll keep that paragraph, since it explains why I’m choosing records rather than just listing equipment.

Leon: For the numbered section, maybe put the checks in the order someone would use them at a shop. I’d start with the sleeve and price, then inspect the record, read the label, and ask to hear it if the store has a listening station.

Mara: I like that sequence. Here’s the revised checklist I’m planning to use:
1. Check the jacket, inner sleeve, and asking price.
2. Inspect the record under a bright light for marks and residue.
3. Confirm the label and catalog number, if they’re visible.
4. Ask whether playback or returns are available before buying.

Priya: That reads clearly. I’d keep “if they’re visible,” since older copies don’t always have the information you’re looking for on the jacket. Also, a listening station can reveal noise, but it won’t tell you how the record sounds on every turntable.

Mara: Thanks, I’ll keep that qualification. I’ll also add a note that I’m sharing my own routine, not a universal grading standard.
